content: Salmonellosis is an infection caused by bacteria belonging to the genus Salmonella. The type of Salmonella most commonly associated with human infections is referred to as Non-Typhoidal Salmonella. This infection is typically acquired through the consumption of raw or undercooked eggs, as well as from sources such as contaminated poultry, cattle, egg products, milk, reptiles carrying the bacteria on their skin, and infected pet rodents. In rare cases, contaminated cannabis has also been linked to outbreaks, such as the Salmonella muenchen outbreak in 1981. The illness typically lasts between 3 to 7 days, and most individuals recover without requiring medical treatment. However, in some cases, the diarrhea can become severe enough to cause dangerous dehydration, necessitating hospitalization. In such situations, patients are treated with intravenous fluids to address dehydration, and medications may be administered to alleviate symptoms such as fever. In severe cases, the infection can spread beyond the intestines to the bloodstream and other parts of the body. If left untreated, this can result in death. Prompt antibiotic treatment is essential in such cases. Populations at higher risk for severe illness include the elderly, infants, and individuals with weakened immune systems. Additionally, some individuals who recover from salmonellosis may later develop reactive arthritis, a condition that can lead to long-term and potentially disabling effects. A less common form of Salmonella infection, caused by Typhoidal Salmonella, can result in typhoid fever. Unlike Non-Typhoidal Salmonella, Typhoidal Salmonella is exclusively carried by humans and is typically transmitted through direct contact with the fecal matter of an infected individual. This form of infection is more prevalent in regions with inadequate sanitation systems for managing human waste. In the United States, the most frequently encountered Salmonella serotypes are Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Enteritidis. The bacteria were first identified over a century ago by an American scientist named Salmon, after whom they are named. Annually, approximately 40,000 cases of salmonellosis are reported in the United States. However, due to underreporting and undiagnosed mild cases, the actual number of infections is estimated to be at least 30 times higher. Salmonellosis is more prevalent during the summer months compared to winter. Children under the age of five are particularly susceptible, with infection rates in this age group being significantly higher than in other populations. Severe infections are more likely to occur in young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals. Each year, an estimated 400 deaths in the United States are attributed to acute salmonellosis. National surveillance systems, such as the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) and FoodNet, monitor culture-confirmed cases of salmonellosis. These systems rely on active laboratoryand population-based surveillance to track the disease. The causative agents of salmonellosis are gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria belonging to the family Enterobacteriaceae. There are approximately 2,000 serotypes of Salmonella capable of causing disease in humans. Transmission occurs through the consumption of contaminated food or water, or through direct contact with infected animals. The natural course of salmonellosis can vary. While most cases resolve without complications, some may result in chronic arthritis or other long-term sequelae. Fatal outcomes are rare but do occur, with an estimated 400 deaths annually in the United States. The diagnosis of salmonellosis is based on clinical history and symptoms. Common symptoms include diarrhea, which may occasionally be bloody, fever, and abdominal cramps. In some cases, the infection can localize to specific areas, such as joints, or enter the bloodstream, leading to more severe manifestations.
